title: Aristotle's Four Causes
objective: After this level you can use Aristotle's four causes (material, formal, efficient and final) to explain what a bronze statue is and why it exists.
summary: Aristotle explained a bronze statue by four causes: the bronze (material), its shape (formal), the art of bronze-casting (efficient) and the finished statue everything is done for (final).

cards.headline: Ask “Why is there a statue?” and Aristotle hands you four answers.
cards.body: Not four guesses: four different kinds of “because”. A full explanation can use all four.

cards.headline: Made of what? Shaped as what?
cards.body: Aristotle held that you only know a thing when you grasp its cause, its “why”. A why-question has more than one kind of answer, so his four causes are four kinds of explanation. Take a bronze statue. The material cause answers “What is it made of?” The bronze. The formal cause answers “What is it?” Its form: the shape the melted bronze is poured into, which makes this lump a statue and not a doorstop.

cards.headline: Made by what? Made for what?
cards.body: The efficient cause answers “Where did the change come from?” Aristotle’s precise answer is the art of bronze-casting, the know-how in the sculptor. The final cause is what it’s for. A model is made, a mold prepared, the bronze melted and poured: every step is done for the sake of the finished statue.

mascot.line: Keep the four questions: made of what, what is it, made by what, and made for what?

cards.headline: Form, but not in the sky
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s Forms? Aristotle studied at Plato’s Academy, yet he rejected Forms that exist apart from things. For him, form lives in the thing itself. In a bronze sphere, the bronze and the roundness aren’t two separate things. Melt the sphere, and its roundness doesn’t float off to another world.

cards.headline: Bacon wants one cause out
cards.body: Not everyone wanted all four. In 1605, Francis Bacon argued that final causes belong to metaphysics, not physics. Saying clouds are “for” watering the earth, he complained, had held back the search for real physical causes. Physics, for Bacon, should stick to material and efficient causes: what things are made of and what moves them.

cards.headline: Aristotle's Four Causes: the big picture
learned: Efficient: where the change came from

questions.prompt: Of Aristotle’s four causes, the one that answers “What is it for?” is the _____ cause.

options.label: formal
options.rationale: That’s what it is, its form.

options.label: efficient
options.rationale: That’s where the change came from.

questions.explanation: The final cause is that for the sake of which something is done, like the finished statue every step aims at.

questions.prompt: Match each of Aristotle’s four causes with the question it answers.

pairs.right: Where did the change come from?

questions.explanation: The material cause answers “What is it made of?”, the formal cause “What is it?”, the efficient cause “Where did the change come from?”, and the final cause is what it’s for.

questions.prompt: How does Aristotle’s idea of form differ from Plato’s Forms?

options.label: Aristotle’s forms are eternal and live apart
Aristotle said forms exist only in words
Aristotle thought form was the same as matter
options.rationale: Form and matter differ, but aren’t separate things.

options.label: Aristotle’s form exists in the thing itself, not a separate world

questions.explanation: Aristotle rejected separately existing Forms: a bronze sphere’s roundness is in the bronze, not in another realm.
